title: What is the difference between a Service Registry and Service Discovery?
shortTitle: The difference between a Service Registry and Service Discovery

s1_definition.profdef: A Service Registry is the component that stores the authoritative, live list of which service instances exist and where they are, meaning their network addresses and health status. Service Discovery is the process and mechanism by which a client finds a healthy instance of a service it wants to call, by consulting that registry. In short, the registry is the data store, the phone book of running instances, while discovery is the act of looking up and resolving a logical service name to an actual address. One is the thing, the other is the activity that uses the thing.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India has many loan officers scattered across branches, and they change desks constantly. The Service Registry is the central directory book at reception that always lists exactly which loan officers are on duty right now and at which desk. Service Discovery is what a customer actually does when they ask reception "where is an available loan officer?" and reception looks in the directory and points them to a free one. The directory book is the registry; the act of asking and being pointed to the right desk is discovery.
s1_definition.oneliner: The Service Registry is the live database of service instances and their addresses, and Service Discovery is the process of querying that registry to resolve a service name into a healthy instance to call.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Service Registry is the component that stores the authoritative, live list of which service instances exist and where they are, meaning their network addresses and health status. Service Discovery is the process and mechanism by which a client finds a healthy instance of a service it wants to call, by consulting that registry. In short, the registry is the data store, the phone book of running instances, while discovery is the act of looking up and resolving a logical service name to an actual address. One is the thing, the other is the activity that uses the thing.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India has many loan officers scattered across branches, and they change desks constantly. The Service Registry is the central directory book at reception that always lists exactly which loan officers are on duty right now and at which desk. Service Discovery is what a customer actually does when they ask reception "where is an available loan officer?" and reception looks in the directory and points them to a free one. The directory book is the registry; the act of asking and being pointed to the right desk is discovery.

**One line to remember:** The Service Registry is the live database of service instances and their addresses, and Service Discovery is the process of querying that registry to resolve a service name into a healthy instance to call.

sections.s2_technical:
Start with why either exists. In microservices, instances are dynamic: they scale up and down, move hosts, restart, and fail. Hardcoding a service's address does not work because the address changes constantly. So you need a live directory of where everything is, and a way to look things up in it. Those two needs are the registry and discovery respectively.

The Service Registry is the authoritative store. Each service instance, when it starts, registers itself by telling the registry its logical name, its network address and port, and often metadata and a health status. It then sends periodic heartbeats so the registry knows it is still alive; if the heartbeats stop, the registry removes or marks the instance as down. Examples of registries are Eureka, Consul, etcd, and the built-in registry behind Kubernetes services. The registry's job is simply to hold an accurate, current list and prune dead instances.

Service Discovery is the lookup process built on top of the registry, and it comes in two main patterns. In client-side discovery, the calling service itself queries the registry, gets the list of healthy instances for the target service, and uses a load-balancing rule to pick one, then calls it directly. Spring Cloud with Eureka plus a client-side load balancer works this way; a call to `lb://payment-service` triggers the client to resolve payment-service against the registry and choose an instance. In server-side discovery, the client just calls a stable address, such as a load balancer or the gateway, and that intermediary consults the registry and routes to an instance, so the client does not talk to the registry at all. Kubernetes services and many cloud load balancers use this model.

So the difference is one of role. The registry answers the question "what instances of service X exist and are they healthy?" and it is a piece of infrastructure that stores state. Discovery answers the question "given that I want to call service X, which concrete instance do I actually send this request to?" and it is a behavior that consumes the registry's state. You cannot have discovery without a registry to consult, but the registry by itself does nothing useful until some discovery process queries it.

Health and freshness tie them together. The registry must track health through heartbeats and health checks so that discovery never hands out a dead instance. There is usually a small staleness window, because it takes a heartbeat or two to notice an instance died, which is why discovery is combined with resilience like retries and circuit breakers so that occasionally being routed to a just-died instance is handled gracefully.

A senior nuance is the relationship with the API Gateway and load balancing. The gateway uses discovery to resolve the backend it routes to, and client-side load balancing is the step inside discovery that picks among the instances the registry returned. Another nuance is consistency versus availability: registries like Eureka favor availability, preferring to return possibly-stale data rather than refuse, which suits service discovery where approximate freshness is fine, whereas a strongly consistent store like etcd makes different trade-offs. The practical point is that the registry is the source of truth about instances, and discovery is the glue that turns a logical service name into a real, reachable, healthy endpoint.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India runs several instances of its payment service, and they scale up at month-end and scale down afterward, and occasionally an instance crashes. The account service needs to call the payment service, but it cannot hardcode an address because the set of live instances keeps changing. We need a live directory and a way to look up a healthy instance.

Problem 2 — When a payment instance dies, callers must stop being sent to it quickly, and new instances that come online must start receiving traffic automatically. This requires registration, heartbeats, health tracking in the registry, and discovery that only returns healthy instances.

The connection to the fix: we will build a simple registry where instances register, send heartbeats, and are pruned when heartbeats stop, and a discovery client that resolves a service name to a healthy instance using load balancing. The demo registers payment instances, discovers one, simulates an instance dying and being pruned, and shows discovery routing only to the survivors.

What the code will do. There is a `ServiceInstance` with a service name, instance ID, address, and last-heartbeat time. There is a `ServiceRegistry` that supports register, heartbeat, deregister, pruning of stale instances, and a query for healthy instances of a service. There is a `DiscoveryClient` that queries the registry and uses round-robin load balancing to pick an instance. There is an `AccountService` that discovers and calls the payment service. The demo registers three payment instances, makes several discovered calls, lets one instance miss heartbeats and get pruned, and shows discovery adapting.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is three payment-service instances registering, followed by discovered calls, a crash, a prune, and a scale-up.

Step 1. The three payment instances register themselves with the registry, each giving its name, instance ID, and address. The registry now holds an authoritative list: pay-1, pay-2, and pay-3, all marked up. This list is the registry's state; nothing has been discovered yet.

Step 2. The account service makes four calls to the payment service. Each call triggers discovery: the discovery client queries the registry for the healthy instances of payment-service, gets all three, and uses round-robin to pick one. So the four calls rotate across pay-1, pay-2, pay-3, and pay-1 again. This is discovery consuming the registry's state to resolve a name to a concrete instance.

Step 3. The pay-2 instance crashes and stops sending heartbeats, while pay-1 and pay-3 keep heartbeating. The registry's prune step notices that pay-2's lease has expired because its last heartbeat is too old, and it removes pay-2 from the directory. The registry's list now accurately reflects only the live instances. Notice the registry did this on its own; discovery was not involved in the pruning.

Step 4. The account service makes four more calls. Now discovery queries the registry and gets only pay-1 and pay-3, because pay-2 is gone. Round-robin rotates between just those two survivors, so no call is ever sent to the dead pay-2. Discovery automatically adapted because the registry's state changed.

Step 5. A new instance, pay-4, scales up and registers itself. The registry adds it to the directory. The next discovered calls now include pay-4 in the round-robin, so the fresh instance starts receiving traffic immediately with no configuration change anywhere. This full cycle shows the clean split: the registry is the evolving source of truth about instances, and discovery is the repeated act of resolving the service name against whatever the registry currently holds.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A Service Registry and Service Discovery are related but distinct, and the cleanest way to say it is that the registry is a thing and discovery is an activity. The Service Registry is the authoritative, live directory that stores which instances of each service exist, their network addresses, and their health. Service Discovery is the process by which a caller resolves a logical service name into a concrete, healthy instance by consulting that registry. You cannot have discovery without a registry to look things up in, and the registry by itself does nothing useful until some discovery process queries it.

The reason both exist is that microservice instances are dynamic. They scale up and down, restart, move hosts, and fail, so their addresses change constantly and hardcoding them is impossible. In my banking work at National Bank of India, we run several instances of the payment service that scale up at month-end and scale down afterward. Each instance registers itself with the registry when it starts, giving its name, address, and health, and then sends periodic heartbeats; if the heartbeats stop, the registry prunes that instance so the directory stays accurate. That registration, heartbeat, and pruning is entirely the registry's job, and tools like Eureka, Consul, etcd, or the mechanism behind Kubernetes services play that role.

Discovery is the lookup built on top. When the account service needs to call the payment service, it does not use a fixed address; it asks discovery to resolve the name payment-service, which queries the registry for the currently healthy instances and then uses a load-balancing rule to pick one. In Spring Cloud this is exactly what a call to lb://payment-service does. There are two flavors: client-side discovery, where the calling service itself queries the registry and picks an instance, and server-side discovery, where the client just calls a stable address like a load balancer or gateway that consults the registry on its behalf. Either way, when the payment instance died, discovery automatically stopped routing to it because the registry had pruned it, and when a new instance scaled up and registered, discovery started sending it traffic immediately, with no configuration change anywhere.

The nuances I always mention are health, freshness, and the tie to the gateway. The registry tracks liveness through heartbeats, but there is a small staleness window, because it takes a heartbeat or two to notice a death, so I always pair discovery with resilience like retries and circuit breakers to handle the rare case of being routed to a just-died instance. I also point out that the gateway uses discovery to resolve the backends it routes to, and that client-side load balancing is really the instance-picking step inside discovery. And registries make deliberate consistency trade-offs; Eureka, for example, favors availability and may return slightly stale data rather than refuse, which is the right trade for discovery because approximate freshness is fine when combined with retries. The bottom line I leave the interviewer with is that the registry is the source of truth about instances, and discovery is the glue that turns a logical service name into a real, reachable, healthy endpoint.
